items.context:
You re-test fifty more cylinders of concrete mixes you have already tested. Which part of
the uncertainty in the strength prediction for those mixes goes down?
items.why:
Repeats pin down the strength of those mixes, so what the model does not know shrinks.
The scatter between repeat specimens is the noise itself, and no number of repeats
removes it from the next specimen.
items.true: Epistemic: the model learns those mixes better
false: Aleatoric: repeated tests average the scatter away
Both, by the same amount
Neither, because the mixes are not new

items.context:
You need to know whether the next cylinder of a mix will pass a strength specification.
Which interval answers that?
items.why:
The cylinder that gets tested is a new measurement, carrying the noise as well as the
model's uncertainty about the mean. A confidence or credible interval covers only the true
function value, so it is narrower than what the specimen will do.
items.true: A prediction interval, which includes the scatter of a new specimen
false: A confidence interval on the mean strength of the mix
A credible interval on the model's parameters
Any of them, since all three are the same width

items.context:
A forecaster ignores the mix and issues the same interval for every cylinder, the 5% to 95%
range of all past strengths. Its 90% intervals cover about 90% of new cylinders. What is
wrong with it?
items.why:
This is the climatological forecaster. Calibration alone can be bought with width; the goal
is the sharpest intervals that stay calibrated. On the concrete data it covered 91% with
intervals 55.9 MPa wide, against 22.2 MPa for the rescaled ensemble.
items.true: It is calibrated but not sharp: its intervals are too wide to be useful
false: Nothing; it is calibrated, so it is a good forecast
It is miscalibrated, because it ignores the inputs
It is sharp but not calibrated

items.context:
On the calibration mixes, the z-scores (y − μ)/σ of an ensemble have a mean square well
above 1. You rescale every σ by the factor that minimizes the negative log likelihood.
What happens to the intervals?
items.why:
The best factor is the root mean square of the calibration z-scores. A mean square above 1
means the errors are larger than the stated σ, so the model was overconfident and the
factor widens every interval.
items.true: They get wider, because the factor is above 1
false: They get narrower, because the factor is below 1
They stay the same width and shift toward the data
Nothing, because rescaling cannot change coverage

items.context:
With its kernel settings held fixed, what does a Gaussian process's predictive variance
depend on?
items.why:
The variance formula contains the kernel values between inputs and no y at all. At fixed
settings a GP that fits badly reports the same band as one that fits well; y reaches the
band only through fitted hyperparameters.
items.true: Only the inputs and the kernel, not the observed targets
false: The training targets, so a poor fit widens the band
The residuals of the mean on the training points
The number of points only, not where they are

items.context:
A team adds more simulation runs to an RBF Gaussian process and notices the fitted length
scale falls every time: 0.09, then 0.06, then 0.03. They conclude the model is resolving
finer detail. What did they miss?
items.true: A length scale that keeps shrinking signals a kernel that does not fit the function, such as a step
false: Nothing; a shorter length scale always means a better model
The optimizer is failing to converge as the data grow
The noise level is too high for an RBF kernel

items.context:
Why is a Gaussian process fitted to five points, with its settings chosen by maximum
likelihood, often overconfident?
items.why:
Short and long length scales fit five points about equally, and the uncertainty about which
is right never reaches the band. Over 200 data sets of five points, the median coverage of
a nominal 95% band was 78%.
items.true: Many settings explain five points equally well, and maximum likelihood keeps one as if known
false: Five points are too few to compute a posterior at all
Maximum likelihood always overestimates the noise
The band cannot widen beyond the data with so few points

items.context:
Noise in a data set grows with x. A Gaussian process with one noise level covers 95% over
the whole range. What does checking coverage by region show?
items.why:
One fitted noise level sits between the small and the large noise, so the band is too wide
on the quiet side and too narrow on the noisy side. By third of the range the toy problem
gave 100%, 98% and 88%.
items.true: Too wide where the noise is small, too narrow where it is large
false: 95% everywhere, since the overall number is right
Too narrow where the noise is small, too wide where it is large
Too narrow everywhere, hidden by rounding

items.context:
Ten networks trained from different seeds agree closely inside the training range, and a
95% interval built from their spread alone covers far less than 95% there. Why?
items.why:
Members disagree about the function, not about a new measurement. Inside the data they
agreed to 0.021 while the noise was 0.1, so the spread alone covered 29%; adding a noise
estimate brought it to 93%.
items.true: The spread measures only the epistemic part and leaves out the noise
false: The networks were not trained long enough
Ten members are too few for a stable spread
The spread is too large and overshoots the data

items.context: What does the spread of models refit on bootstrap resamples estimate?
items.why:
Resampling shows how the fit would change with a new data set of the same size. If every
resample makes the same mistake, the spread is small and the error large, so the bias is
missed, and so is the noise.
items.true: How much the fitted function varies with the data: the variance part of the error
false: The noise in a new measurement
The bias of the model, including its errors far from the data
The total prediction error, noise included

items.context:
An optimizer searches a surrogate for the strongest mix it can find, and the team reports
each proposed mix with a split conformal 90% interval, citing the method's finite-sample
guarantee. What is wrong?
items.why:
The guarantee needs only exchangeability, and an optimizer breaks it on purpose. On the
strongest mixes, held out because they differ, split conformal covered 56% at a nominal 90%.
items.true: Proposed mixes are chosen for being different, so they are not exchangeable with the calibration mixes
false: Split conformal needs Gaussian errors, which strengths are not
The calibration set must be larger than the training set
Conformal intervals cannot be used with neural networks

items.context: How does the width of a plain split conformal interval vary across inputs?
items.true: It is the same everywhere; the guarantee holds on average over inputs
false: It grows where the training data are sparse
It follows the noise level at each input
It shrinks as the model becomes more confident

items.context: What coverage does the jackknife+ guarantee for a target level of 1 − α?
items.why:
Barber et al. prove 1 − 2α and show the factor of 2 cannot be removed in general, while
reporting near 1 − α in practice. The plain jackknife has no guarantee, and its coverage can
vanish.
items.true: At least 1 − 2α in the worst case, and close to 1 − α in practice
false: Exactly 1 − α, like split conformal
At least 1 − α, but only with Gaussian errors
No guarantee at all, like the plain jackknife

items.context:
LinearRegressionUQ with a cubic basis, fitted to a sine on [0, 1], covers about 95% inside
the data and almost nothing beyond it, although its band widens there. Why?
items.why:
The parameter term says how unsure the coefficients of a cubic are, not whether a cubic is
the right shape. That is model inadequacy, and nothing inside the training range reveals it.
items.true: The cubic basis is wrong for a sine, and its uncertainty only covers fits within that basis
false: The noise estimate is too small
Linear regression cannot produce prediction intervals
The band widens too fast and overshoots

items.context:
While fitting, a pycse model prints "Model is well-calibrated", then covers well under 95%
beyond its training range. What did the message check?
items.why:
The validation points came from the same range as the training points, so the check is an
in-distribution statement. It says nothing about inputs beyond the data.
items.true: The rescaling factor on validation points from inside the training range
false: Coverage on a held-out region beyond the training data
That the network converged
That the residuals are Gaussian
